title: Rate limiting
short: Cap how often one user can call you, so nobody floods the system.
what: A rate limiter counts requests per user, API key or IP and refuses the extra ones, usually with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. The token bucket is the classic way: allow short bursts, but hold the average to a fixed rate. It protects your servers from bugs, scrapers and attacks.
analogy: A ticket machine at a busy counter that prints 1 ticket a minute and holds at most 5. Arrive in a crowd and the first 5 are served; after that, wait for the next ticket.

frames.label: bucket for API key 42, t = 0 s
frames.say: A weather API gives each key a bucket of 5 tokens. Every request spends one. One token drips back in each second, up to 5.

frames.label: t = 0 s
frames.say: A script sends 3 requests at once. Each takes a token and goes through. Short bursts are fine, up to the bucket size.

frames.label: t = 0 s, bucket empty
frames.say: Then 3 more at once. Two get the last tokens. The third finds the bucket empty and gets 429 Too Many Requests.

frames.label: t = 1 s
frames.say: At t = 1 s one token drips back in. The script retries, and that one request goes through.

frames.label: t = 1 s to 5 s
frames.say: The script keeps firing 10 requests a second. Only 1 a second gets through, the refill rate. Your servers' load stays capped.

frames.label: t = 10 s
frames.say: The script stops for 5 seconds. The bucket refills to 5 and stops there, so even a long break earns at most a burst of 5.

when: A public API must be shared fairly
Bots or scripts could flood you
Login or signup must resist password guessing
A costly backend (payments, SMS) needs protection

watch: With many servers, keep the bucket in a shared store like Redis, or each server allows the full rate.
Tell clients when to retry: send 429 with a Retry-After header.
Limiting only by IP is unfair: a whole office or phone network can share one IP.
interview: Design a login system that stops password guessing
